data.name: Tales of Glacier (VR)
data.detailed_description:
“Tales of Glacier” Background Story and Rules of the Game
It is said that there was a wonder land located in the coldest place of the earth. The indigenous people lived happily under the protect of the God. Until one day, an evil dragon came here leading its vicious corps. Destroying everything violently and expelling the residents out of their home, the evil dragon attempted to occupy the whole world. At this moment, the God came down from heaven and fought a life-and-death battle with the dragon in order to protect the residents. In the end, the dragon was defeated and fled into the ice land with its corps. The world was back in peace. To prevent the dragon from invading again, the God built a magic gate and sent guardians to garrison there. During this short peaceful time, everything was covered by cold thick ice. Turret was frozen and the magic has been weakened. The dragon from afar is getting ready for the next attack. Another protection battle is about to begin.
Operation Instructions:
1. Two-handed Sword: pressing the trigger key of either hilt, waving the hilt rapidly and then loosing the hilt, an attack could be launched. Controlling the hilt and crossing the swords with both hands, a defense could be conducted. Lifting two swords over your head could charge power. After charging for 3 seconds, waving down the swords simultaneously could trigger clutch shot.

2. Wands: the left hilt of magical weapons controls magic book and the right hilt controls wands.Pressing the trigger key of right hilt could charge magic power. Adjusting the position of right hilt could control the cast track. Loosening the trigger key after charging power for 0.5 second could launch the magic according to the cast track. Pressing the trigger key of left hilt could conduct defense but attacks could not be conducted while defensing. Charging magic power for 1.5 seconds or 3 seconds could trigger more powerful magic.
3. Bow and Arrow: left hilt controls the bow and right hilt controls the bowstring. Adjusting the position of left and right hilts and imitating the bow drawing action could control the arrow shooting track. Pressing the trigger key of right hilt and pulling back the right hilt could pull the string. Loosening the trigger key could shoot the arrow according to the shooting track. Pressing the trigger key of left hilt could conduct defense but attacks could not be conducted while defensing. After hitting one target, next attack will become multiple shot attack. Continuous hit will launch the clutch shot of bow and arrow.

reviews.review:
Tales of Glacier (VR) is an early virtual reality action-adventure that takes a simple fantasy conflict and builds it around physical weapon handling. Developed and published by BINGOBELL, it places the player in a frozen land threatened by the return of an evil dragon and its forces. The background gives the adventure a mythological flavor, describing a once-peaceful people protected by a god until an invading dragon brought destruction to their homeland. Although the story establishes the foundations for a much larger fantasy journey, the actual game is considerably smaller and concentrates primarily on combat rather than exploration or narrative development.

Its most interesting quality is the choice of combat styles. Instead of relying on one universal weapon, the game experiments with swords, magic, and archery, with each approach requiring different physical actions from the player. Dual swords are suited to direct close-range encounters, allowing the player to attack by swinging the motion controllers and defend by positioning the weapons appropriately. Stronger attacks can also be prepared through specific movements. The system is uncomplicated compared with newer physics-heavy VR melee games, but the act of physically attacking and defending still provides a satisfying degree of involvement.

Magic changes the rhythm considerably. A book and wand arrangement allows spells to be charged and directed toward enemies, making this style feel less frantic than sword fighting. More powerful attacks require additional preparation, so there is a modest risk-versus-reward element when deciding whether to release a quick spell or spend more time building a stronger one. Defensive actions add another layer to the system, although the mechanics remain fairly basic. The appeal comes primarily from performing the gestures yourself rather than managing complicated statistics or extensive spell combinations.

Archery is perhaps the most immediately natural fit for virtual reality. Drawing the bow with tracked controllers creates a convincing physical interaction, while accuracy is encouraged through bonuses associated with successful attacks. Maintaining good performance can lead to stronger offensive possibilities, giving players an incentive to aim carefully instead of firing arrows without consideration. Moving between sword fighting, spellcasting, and archery gives the experience some welcome variety and demonstrates that the game was designed around VR interaction from the beginning.

The biggest weakness is that these mechanics exist inside a fairly limited overall structure. The frozen fantasy world sounds intriguing from its description, but there is not enough exploration, storytelling, progression, or environmental variety to make it feel like a fully developed adventure. Much of the experience revolves around confronting enemies and experimenting with the available combat methods. Consequently, repetition can appear relatively quickly. A larger campaign with more locations, enemy behaviors, progression systems, and meaningful encounters could have transformed the core mechanics into something considerably more memorable.

Visually, the icy setting provides an appropriate atmosphere for the conflict, even if the presentation now clearly shows the age and modest scale of the project. It originally arrived during an earlier generation of consumer VR gaming, and expectations should be adjusted accordingly. The graphics and interactions lack the refinement associated with more recent VR releases, but the combination of snowy scenery, fantasy creatures, weapons, and magical effects gives the game enough character to establish its intended identity. It works better as a snapshot of experimental early VR design than as a showcase for modern virtual reality technology.

The game is single-player and VR-only, with tracked motion controllers being fundamental to its design. Standing and room-scale VR configurations are supported, reinforcing how dependent the gameplay is on physical interaction. This distinction is particularly important for Steam Deck owners. Tales of Glacier (VR) should be considered unsupported for practical Steam Deck use because it is a VR-only experience requiring SteamVR-style tracked controller interaction. Even though no dedicated Steam Deck compatibility rating is clearly established for the title itself, the Deck is not a substitute for the required PC VR hardware and motion-control setup.

Tales of Glacier (VR) ultimately feels more like a focused VR combat experiment than a complete fantasy epic. There are enjoyable concepts here, particularly in the way the three weapon styles encourage different movements and tactics, and the dragon-centered frozen-world premise gives the action some context. However, limited content, repetitive encounters, basic presentation, and shallow progression keep those ideas from reaching their full potential. For players curious about smaller VR projects from the earlier years of SteamVR, it can still provide an interesting historical experience. Those seeking a deep campaign, sophisticated physics, extensive character progression, or a richly explorable fantasy world will find it much more limited.

Rating: 6/10
